title: Seven seconds is too long
scenario: A software company's support assistant takes too long to reply. The team lists timings and three ideas (exhibit). You choose what to do, and you review one more problem: a report feature that times out.
exhibit:
(made-up example data)

PIPELINE, one request
  S1  input check      0.8 s   (the answer may be shown only if S1 passes)
  S2  retrieve docs    0.5 s
  S3  draft answer     6.0 s   (needs the result of S2)
  steps in a row:      7.3 s   (0.8 + 0.5 + 6.0)

DRAFT STEP (S3)
  now:                 6,000 input tokens, 800 output tokens
  idea A:              cut input to 3,000 tokens
  idea B:              cut output to 400 tokens

NIGHTLY EVAL JOB
  30,000 requests at 01:00, results read the next morning
  idea C:              run it in a fast mode so it ends sooner

MONTHLY REPORT FEATURE
  max_tokens 64,000, no streaming
  error: request timed out after 10 minutes (users on office networks)

questions.prompt: For the draft step, ideas A and B each cut a token count in half. Which helps more?

options.text: Idea A. Prompt size sets how long the whole call takes.
options.explanation: The OpenAI docs say cutting 50% of a prompt may only improve latency by 1 to 5%, unless the context is huge.

options.text: Neither. Larger models usually respond faster, so switch up.
options.explanation: The docs say the opposite: smaller models usually run faster. The Claude docs name Haiku 5.5 for speed-critical apps.

options.text: They help the same, because latency depends on total tokens only.
options.explanation: Output tokens are generated one at a time, so they cost far more time than input tokens.

options.text: Idea B. Generating tokens is the slowest step in a call.
options.explanation: Right. The rule of thumb in the OpenAI docs: cutting 50% of output tokens may cut about 50% of latency.

questions.prompt: S3's answer may be shown only if S1 passes. How can the pipeline get faster?

options.text: Skip the input check, since it adds 0.8 s to every request.
options.explanation: The check protects the product. The trick is to hide its time, not to remove it.

options.text: Stream the draft and keep the steps in a row. Total time falls.
options.explanation: Streaming lets users see the first words sooner, but the total time stays the same.

options.text: Start S1 beside the rest, and cancel the draft if S1 fails.
options.explanation: Right. This is OpenAI's speculative execution. The time becomes about 6.5 s (0.5 + 6.0), because S1's 0.8 s runs alongside.

options.text: Run S3 first because it is longest, then S1 and S2.
options.explanation: S3 needs the result of S2, so it cannot start first.

questions.prompt: Idea C is a fast mode for the 01:00 eval job. What fits the docs?

options.text: Yes. OpenAI's guide recommends Fast mode for large batch jobs.
options.explanation: The OpenAI docs advise the opposite: avoid running large ETL or batch jobs in Fast mode.

options.text: No. A fast mode costs a premium and suits user-facing calls.
options.explanation: Right. Both vendors price fast modes at a premium. Nobody waits for this job, so batch or Flex fits (chapter 2).

options.text: Yes. Claude's fast mode works inside the Batch API and costs less.
options.explanation: Claude's fast mode is not available with the Batch API, and it is priced at a premium.

options.text: Yes. Fast modes are cheaper when used between midnight and 06:00.
options.explanation: The docs describe no time-of-day discount. Fast modes carry a per-token premium.

questions.prompt: The report feature times out at 10 minutes. What is the best fix?

options.text: Stream the response, or use Batch if nobody is waiting.
options.explanation: Right. The Claude docs advise streaming or Batch for long requests, because some networks drop idle connections.

options.text: Raise max_tokens so the reply is finished in one longer call.
options.explanation: A larger max_tokens allows an even longer wait, which makes the timeout more likely.

options.text: Add three retries, so one of the attempts finishes in time.
options.explanation: Each retry has the same long wait. Three timed-out attempts keep the user waiting even longer.

options.text: Cut the request timeout to 60 s so the call fails faster.
options.explanation: That only makes the failure come sooner. The report still does not arrive.
